I've been reading and found out more about the mizuage legend.

In Japan, the term for the underworld is *mizu shobai*, "water trade". This includes and included any after-hours entertainment ranging from geiko in ochaya to hostess bars and prostitution across the different periods in Japanese history.

Beginning in the early Edo period (1600s), the *mizu shobai* was moved out of the cities and put into separate red light districts or *hanamachi*. Differing roles in the hanamachi included:

* ***Yujo*** - Yujo were prostitutes, but were not trained in traditional arts.

* ***Oiran*** - High-class *yujo* from Tokyo. Their primary business was sex, but they were also trained in the arts of the nobility such as tea ceremony, flower arraning, dance, music and incence-burning.

* ***Tayuu*** - Like oiran, tayuu evolved from court culture. Masters of entertainment and highly educated, they entertained their patrons with dance, music and conversation. Tayuu entertained in restaurants called *ageya*, the last of which is the Sumiya in Shimabara. They did not sell sex, so differ from oiran in that regard.

* ***Geiko*** - Geiko evolved from the culture of the common people, so their clothing was more similar to merchants of the time. Geiko entertained in *ochaya*, but also alongside tayuu in *ageya*. The *gokagai* (five hanamachi) in Kyoto evolved from inns along major roadways (Pontocho and Miyagwacho) and inns outside the major temples (Gion, Kamishichiken). The Tokyo regional equivalent is the *geisha*.

* ***Maiko*** - Apprentice geiko. The Tokyo regional equivalent is the *hangyoku*.

For a more in-depth description of these roles, see [here](http://missmyloko.tumblr.com/KaryukaiRoles).

***Mizuage* literally means "hoisting from water". It was the deflowering of a young apprentice *yujo* for money. Sex has never been a part of a geiko or maiko's professional life.**

The coming of age ceremony that a maiko has is called *wage eri*, a celebration of the progress the maiko has made. Her han-eri changes from red to white and her hairstyle changes from wareshinobu to ofuku.

The myth that a maiko's "split peach" hairstyle is a nod to mizuage is silly. The hairstyle they are referring to is momoware, a hairstyle no longer worn by maiko. It is similar to ofuku but really looks nothing like the body anatomy it's said to look like.
